Flatiron Building. The 22-story triangular office building completed in 1902 in Manhattan, located at the intersection of Broadway, Fifth Avenue, and twenty-third Street. Its distinctive wedge shape and Beaux-Arts Renaissance Revival styling make it one of the most iconic and photographed buildings in the world. It was designed by architect Daniel Burnham of the Chicago School, and the building's triangular footprint fills an entire lot where two major streets converge at an acute angle. Standing 307 feet tall, it was among the tallest buildings in the world at its completion and remains one of the most recognizable due to its unique silhouette. The facade of limestone, granite, and terra-cotta features Beaux-Arts detailing with arched windows and ornamental cornices, creating a highly sculptural appearance. Named for its resemblance to a clothes iron, particularly when viewed from afar, the building's pointed north edge created wind vortexes that caused skirts to blow up, earning it early notoriety. The triangular plan was an engineering feat for its time, requiring careful structural calculation to distribute loads across the narrow footprint. Originally headquarters for the Fuller Company but became best known as an architectural monument and tourist destination, featured in countless photographs and artworks.
